quote: What subjects tended to do instead, however, was match probabilities—that is, predict the more probable event with the relative frequency with which it occurred.
content: Claim: in binary prediction with base-rate predictability, subjects "match probabilities" rather than maximize. Probability matching is a real and frequently-observed phenomenon, documented since the 1950s (Estes, 1950; reviewed by Vulkan, 2000, https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-6419.00106). However, it is not universal or fixed: maximization increases markedly with financial incentives, with clearer feedback, when subjects deliberate rather than respond intuitively (Koehler & James, 2009, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2009.03.009), and even across species and developmental stages. So the effect is robust as a default tendency but strongly moderated by task conditions, contrary to a reading of it as an immutable flaw.

Claim: even paid subjects over a thousand trials chose the majority option only about 76% of the time. The specific figure traces to Tversky & Edwards (1966), "Information versus reward in binary choices," https://doi.org/10.1037/h0023123. The qualitative result (sub-maximizing despite payment) replicates, but later work shows the magnitude is sensitive to incentive size and design; in some paradigms a substantial fraction of subjects do converge toward maximization (Shanks, Tunney & McCarthy, 2002, https://doi.org/10.1002/bdm.413). The cited number is a single study's value, not a fixed constant.

quote: I would suspect that something simpler is going on—that the all-blue strategy just didn’t occur to the subjects.
content: Claim: the maximizing ("all-blue") strategy simply did not occur to subjects, rather than reflecting overconfidence. This is a plausible interpretation and aligns with research suggesting probability matching arises partly from an effortful but mistaken search for patterns in random sequences (Wolford et al., 2004, on pattern-seeking; Gaissmaier & Schooler, 2008, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2008.02.002, who found matching correlates with attempts to detect sequential structure). The pattern-search account has empirical support, but the specific introspective claim ("just didn't occur to them") is an inference; competing accounts (e.g., expectation-matching heuristics) also fit the data.

Claim: randomizing your actions is unconditionally irrational — "a random key does not open a random lock," so matching only ever makes you "stupid." This holds in the essay's stipulated setup (an i.i.d. sequence, fixed payoff for accuracy, no observer), but stated as a general principle it is false: in adversarial and strategic environments randomization is provably optimal. The minimax theorem (von Neumann, 1928; see Osborne & Rubinstein, 1994, A Course in Game Theory) shows that against an opponent who can exploit any predictable pure strategy — matching pennies, rock-paper-scissors, penalty kicks — the unique optimal play is a deliberately mixed (randomized) strategy, and field studies confirm expert players approximate it (Chiappori, Levitt & Groseclose, 2002, on soccer penalties, https://doi.org/10.1257/000282802762024611). Probability matching can likewise be ecologically rational when payoffs depend on others' choices or on covering a distribution of states rather than guessing a single hidden constant. "Fight fire with water" is good advice against a static random source; it is bad advice against an adaptive adversary.

Claim: this single experiment "compactly illustrates the most important idea in all of rationality" — that the optimal response to a foggy world is to behave lawfully, never to inject chaos. The rhetorical elevation outruns what one binary-prediction paradigm can bear, and it quietly smuggles in the strong assumption that the environment is genuinely structureless and non-strategic. Real "uncertain worlds" are frequently the opposite — partially observable, non-stationary, and populated by other agents — settings in which the rational policy can involve exploration, hedging, and randomization rather than repeating the current point-estimate of the best action (the explore/exploit tradeoff in bandit problems, Sutton & Barto, 2018, Reinforcement Learning). Even Bayesian decision theory only prescribes "always take the currently-best action" once you have already conditioned on a model; while learning, deterministically exploiting can be strictly suboptimal. The deep lesson is real for the stated game, but "never randomize" is a domain-specific result dressed up as a universal law of reason.
